newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian Oil Corp pressing ahead with refinery plans.
newsitem.headline: Indian Oil Corp pressing ahead with refinery plans.

text.p: Indian Oil Corp (IOC) is pressing ahead with various refinery projects to help meet India's growing demand for petroleum products, A.K. Arora, director of refineries and pipelines said on Thursday.
In an interview with Reuters, he detailed some of the projects as India seeks to double its refining capacity in the next five years to 2.5 million barrels per day (bpd).
"We should be at almost equal capacity (again) by 2001/2," he said, referring to plans to boost capacity to meet growing demand.
India's Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas has said demand for petroleum products is growing at a compound seven percent per year.
The ministry forecasts demand for products would nearly double in the next 10 years to 3.2 million bpd in 2006/7 from 1.65 million bpd now.
"Until now the refinery capacity has been lagging. The demand has always been beating it," Arora said. "But at least the initial plan is now there to double capacity."
IOC is spending 100 billion rupees on projects already underway and has earmarked another 250 billion for planned projects, the state-owned oil company said in October.

India has 14 refineries producing around 1.25 million bpd, but must still import about 400,000 bpd to meet its needs. Its purchases can have a major impact on European, Mediterranean and Far East oil markets.

IOC, which is 91.14 percent government controlled, operates six of the refineries with a combined refining capacity of just under 500,000 bpd. The remaining refineries are owned by various other companies.

IOC has signed a memorandum of understanding with the Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC) to build a 250,000 bpd refinery in Paradeep on the east coast, which should be on stream by the turn of the century, Arora said.
Arora said a feasibility study for the refinery project has been completed and will be submitted for approvals by the IOC board and then the Indian government.
He said IOC and KPC were now working on prequalification documents for the engineering and construction of the refinery.
Arora also said IOC and Malaysian state oil company Petronas were discussing plans to build a 120,000 bpd refinery at Nagapattinam on the south east coast.

He said the talks were conceptual at this stage, but they involved gearing the refinery 75 percent to exports and 25 percent to sales to the domestic Indian market. The plant could be operational early in the next decade.
The company was also carrying out exploratory talks with Japan's Marubeni Corp. covering upstream and downstream ventures, including the potential for a petrochemical project.
He said a potential tie up would most likely occur in India, but added that a project outside the country was not out of the question.
Arora said the IOC was also working to expand existing refineries, with current output of 205,000 bpd, up to 265,000 bpd.
Its planned 1,132 kilometre Haldia-to-Barauni pipeline in the northeast would allow the Barauni refinery to expand output to 85,000 bpd from its current operating rate of 40,000 bpd, Arora said.
The pipeline is scheduled for completion by 1999.
Arora said the output of the refinery would then be expanded to 125,000 bpd.
The 70,000 bpd Haldia refinery would also be expanded to 90,000 bpd sometime in 1997, Arora said.
